newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices jump to eight-month high.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices jump to eight-month high.

text.p: Coffee prices rose to eight-month highs Tuesday as speculators bought heavily on worries that supplies were falling faster than expected.
In other markets, rallies in lumber and corn helped offset weakness in oil markets. The Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures closed 0.91 point higher at 242.31.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March coffee futures ended 3.75 cents per pound higher at 122.20 cents, its highest settlement since May 17.
"Overall stocks are low," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Predergast. "CSCE stocks are low, consumer stocks are low, and producer stocks are low."

Supply jitters were fuelled by the latest drop in stocks certified for delivery at the CSCE. The exchange reported after Monday's close that certified stocks in U.S. warehouses fell by 9,070 60-kilogram bags in the week ended Jan. 10 to to 23,388 bags.
Traders await the Green Coffee Association of New York's monthly stock report for December, due after Wednesday's close, to get a broader picture of the supply situation.

Most expected the data to show an increase of some 50,000 to 100,000 bags in the month, although some traders forecasted a decline of up to 150,000 bags. In November, Green Coffee Association stocks rose by 4,000 bags to 1,264,000 bags.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber futures pared gains at the close as commercial firms sold into a rally fed by speculator buying. January lumber closed $4.50 higher at $405.00 per thousand board feet, down from a $412 high.
"Prices are still too high to accumulate spring inventory," said Curt Cunningham of Pacific Futures Trading.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn ended mostly higher with professional investors such as commodity funds buying contracts to cover earlier "short" positions.
March corn rose 3-1/2 cents to end at $2.70-3/4 a bushel.

Traders pointed out that many funds had sold corn contracts heading into last Friday's monthly Agriculture Department crop report -- which turned out to show lower than expected grain production and stockpiles, and drove futures higher.
"They covered another 50 million bushels. They covered about 50 million Friday and more today," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor and Co.

Soybeans ended mixed, with January up 1 cent per bushel at $7.33-3/4. Soybeans were pressured early by forecasts for rain in the key Brazilian soybean region of Rio Grande do Sul, but later reports suggested rains would likely miss parched growing regions.
Brazil, which plants grain crops in the fall, is the leading rival of the United States for soy exports.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices fell as traders expected weekly oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute to show significant rises.
"There was some position-squaring ahead of the API stats tonight. We expect crude stocks will grow after falling so much last week," said Tom Bentz, analyst with ING Derivatives.

February unleaded gasoline led the declines, ending down 1.05 cents a gallon at 67.04 cents. February crude ended off 8 cents a barrel at $25.11 and February heating oil down 0.28 cent a gallon at 69.42 cents.
After the close, the API said crude oil stocks rose 4.65 million barrels in the week ended Jan. 10, against forecasts for a rise of at least two million.

Gasoline stocks rose 415,000 barrels in the week, while traders expected a rise of 2 million barrels. Distillate stocks, which include heating oil and diesel, fell 1.29 million barrels. The fall and renewed cold weather in the Northeast should support prices, analysts said.

"The short-term (weather) forecasts are definitely supportive right now, though we are seeing some follow-through selling in crude after yesterday's decline," said trader Michael Busby with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.
